meta.title: Comping a Whole Song
meta.summary: I V vi IV as four grips inside four frets, voice-led, then the half that isn't shapes at all — muting, one string set, and where the strikes land.

spans.text: . It is the four-chord loop popular music keeps coming back to, and you have probably played it a hundred times with barre chords, crossing the neck to do it. On strings 1-2-3, taking the nearest inversion each time, the whole thing lives between fret 3 and fret 6.

props.caption: A minor, first inversion, strings 1-2-3 — the only grip in this loop with all three notes at the same fret.

spans.text: Four grips inside four frets is not a part yet. A part is the grips plus the muting plus where the strikes land, and the second two are where most of the sound actually comes from.

items.text: Mute.
The fretting hand relaxes the instant after the strike, so the chord stops dead. The click that's left behind is part of the part, not a mistake you're failing to clean up.
Keep the picking hand on one set.

Working the same three strings for a whole passage, rather than roving, is what makes the muting reliable — and it's the practical reason three-string triads became a rhythm-guitar habit as much as a fretting choice.
Put the chords where the rhythm wants them.
Not on every beat. A comping part is mostly silence with chords placed into it.

spans.text: Nile Rodgers has said he was taught to play chords in sets of three strings by Ted Dunbar — Wes Montgomery's old roommate — and that the muted, percussive attack came from Chic's bassist Bernard Edwards. That is his own account of how he learned it rather than a transcription of the records, which is worth knowing, but it is a first-hand description of exactly this technique.

items.text: One chord per bar, four bars, quarter-note downstrokes, slow enough that no change is rushed.
Strikes on beats 2 and 4 only, everything else muted. The silence is the hard part.
Eighth notes, with the chord landing on the offbeats — the "and" rather than the number.

Read a chart's slash and know both what it asks for and who it is asking.
Voice-lead a progression so that no hand jumps and something is usually held.

spans.text: What comes next, and it is out of scope here, is the spread or open-voiced triad — the same three notes with one of them lifted an octave, so the grip skips a string.

All those grips were never really the point. The point is the thing underneath them: a chord is three notes, those three notes exist in several places at once, and you can now put them wherever the music has room for them.
